source.title: How do Scaling Laws Apply to Knowledge Graph Engineering Tasks? The Impact of Model Size on Large Language Model Performance
source.authors: Desiree Heim; Lars-Peter Meyer; Markus Schröder; Johannes Frey; Andreas Dengel

record.tranche_reason: The study measures benchmark task scores across model-size categories and model families, rather than measuring held-out pretraining cross-entropy or fitting the original scaling-law equations.
record.gate_note: The study reports downstream benchmark scores by model-size category and by individual model/family. Rows below record the size-category means from Table 3. It also describes family-level score drops, plateaus, ceiling effects, and lack of clear parallelism between families; figure-specific individual model values are not extracted. Its size-category means are averages across models, not individual model results.
record.test_reason: The study tests V6 in a new downstream setting: knowledge graph engineering tasks across 26 open instruction-tuned models of 0.5–72B parameters. It measures size–performance associations, but fits no predictive scaling rule. It does not test V7: differences in benchmark scores are not evidence about fitted scaling exponents, compute allocation, or departures from a fitted power law.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially accurate: larger open models usually perform better, with local within-family drops and plateau or ceiling effects that can favour smaller models. The authors also report persistent difficulty on RdfFriendCount and Text2Sparql. Their suggestion that proprietary models are much larger is an assumption: proprietary parameter counts are explicitly undocumented.
record.recipe_differences: Compares downstream KGE benchmark scores across pre-existing model-size categories and families; it does not measure held-out loss or train scaling runs.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary by task and input variation; the authors also report local family-level drops, plateau/ceiling effects, and no clear global parallelism between families.
record.peer_reviewed: ESWC 2025 Workshops and Tutorials Joint Proceedings; the text states it is peer reviewed and to appear.
record.problems: Only 26 open models up to 72B parameters are included in the main size analysis; results concern downstream KGE tasks, not pretraining loss. The analysis groups models into broad size bands, uses one benchmark run, and does not fit power laws or test extrapolation. Exact standard deviations for the Table 3 category means are not supplied there, and figure-level per-model values are not extracted.
record.rows_left_out: Table 3 rows for the remaining task variations are omitted to stay within the 60-row limit and prioritize unusual, plateau, and representative increasing patterns. Omitted variations include RdfConnectionExplain nt/turtle/xml; RdfSyntaxFixing nt/turtle; Sparql2Answer turtle; SparqlSyntaxFixing turtle; Text2Answer turtle; and additional variations listed in Table 3. Figure 1 individual-model scores and family-level comparisons are described qualitatively but not extracted as numerical rows.

untested.parts: Held-out pretraining loss and power-law dependence on parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of much larger runs from laws fitted on smaller runs.
Fixed-compute optimisation and parameter/token allocation exponents.
Controlled architecture comparisons at fixed parameter count.
Power-law scaling in other modalities or training regimes; evaluating instruction-tuned models does not itself test such a law.
Quantitative predictive rules, held-out prediction of unseen models, dependence on pretraining loss, and controlled isolation of parameter scale from training data and model family.
Dependence of fitted exponents or compute-optimal splits on setup or fitting choices, and departures from a fitted single power law.

record.verdict_notes: All row links to V7 should be removed. States use a stated smaller-size comparison, not absolute task accuracy; tiny rows serve as reference values. Category means mix model families and training histories, so they establish associations rather than a controlled causal scaling law. Failure to reject a group difference does not establish equivalence. Individual-model and family results are already declared in rows_left_out, so they are not listed as missing.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss and power-law relationships in parameters, training tokens, or training compute.
Whether laws fitted on small runs predict substantially larger runs.
Compute-budget allocation, compute-optimal parameter and token counts, and their exponents.
Controlled comparisons of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Other modalities and training regimes, including repeated data, fine-tuning, and transfer as scaling-law tests.
The study measures KGE downstream benchmark scores against model size, but does not test their predictability from pretraining loss or fit a downstream prediction rule.
It reports plateaus, local drops, and different score developments across tasks/families, but does not estimate scaling exponents, compare fitting methods, or test compute-optimal splits.
